title: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents
body: Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents See how developers are combining AI agents with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build simulation applications, test physical behavior and guide improvements. November 19, 2026 by NVIDIA Writers 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! Your browser doesn't support HTML5 video. Here is a link to the video instead. Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs. Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities. Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem. Physical AI Paves the Path to Autonomous Industrial Operations 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Nyhamna_footage_take5_30s.mp4 AI agents powered by frontier models pave the way to autonomous operations. They use industrial tools and engineering data to help engineers build digital twins that test plans and processes and evaluate operational decisions. Falkor, a KONGSBERG company, shows how this works in practice. The company’s Falkor Surface platform lets customers turn their computer-aided design and engineering data into facility-scale digital twins using the GPT-6 Astra model. The platform uses NVIDIA Omniverse libraries and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Server Edition GPUs on Microsoft Azure to enable advanced physics simulation. AI agents built on Falkor’s agentic engine understand dense technical documentation, spatial relationships and real-world physics. Engineers can create and test plans in simulation before traveling on site, reducing costly delays and mistakes. They can also inspect equipment and check clearances in a shared view. Read Falkor’s article and watch the livestream f or a closer look at how the company builds these tools and checks the agents’ work. Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation With SimReady Assets 🔗 Getting a robot model into a scene is only the start. Developers also need to assemble its components, add controls and check whether it can complete a task. NVIDIA developers Dillon Bailey and Rishabh Chadha used 3D assets from the SimReady Central library to build a pick-and-place simulation of a robot moving a can using the NVIDIA Isaac Sim framework. They directed an agent equipped with GPT-6 Sol and Isaac Sim skills to assemble the scene and generate pick-and-place controls. Testing the assembled scene shows how the assets work together, from joint movement and contact behavior to the gripper’s ability to hold, move and release the can. With that baseline in place, developers can adjust object positions and motion paths and repeat the tests to evaluate how each change affects the task. Follow the walkthrough to assemble and test a pick-and-place simulation in Isaac Sim, with sample agent prompts and checks for robot movement and grasp behavior. Build a Voice-Controlled VR Simulation With SimReady Assets 🔗 Bringing 3D assets into virtual reality (VR) requires more than rendering a scene. Objects need to respond to controllers and behave as expected when grabbed, moved or released. NVIDIA Omniverse community developer Michael Wagner took on this challenge. He directed GPT-6 Astra to use Blender software to model a study environment from two reference images, balancing visual quality with efficient performance in VR. He then used Claude Code to build an application that lets users find SimReady Central assets by voice and interact with them in an immersive VR scene. The Claude Code agent worked for about eight hours, and Wagner built the application over a weekend using an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada workstation and a Meta Quest 3 VR headset. The application ran on NVIDIA Omniverse libraries : ovstage shared the OpenUSD scene, ovrtx rendered it, ovxr enabled VR and ovphysx ran physics. Wagner later built a second version with ovnewton , which integrates with ovstage, to compare the physics libraries. The biggest challenge for Wagner was checking what happened inside the headset. Automated tests missed problems he could feel, including objects shaking when grabbed. Wagner reported the symptoms, guided the agent through changes and verified the interaction himself. Updating the grab control once per frame resolved the shaking. His takeaway: Give agents renders and logs to inspect, then check the experience directly. Explore his open source demo f or build instructions, a starting prompt and reusable agent skills. Send Microducks on Rounds in a Simulated Hospital 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/microducks-icu-16x9-1920x1080-new.mp4 Before adapting a robot to a new environment, developers need to test whether its walking policy — the AI that controls how it moves — can keep it stable in that setting. AI developer Maziyar Panahi directed Claude Code, using Claude Opus 5.5, to assemble an intensive care unit from 13 NVIDIA SimReady hospital assets and test Microduck robots inside it. The assets came with Newton physics settings, so Panahi didn’t have to model the furniture or create collision geometry from scratch. The Newton physics engine also helped replicate the ward so hundreds of copies could run together on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU. When the cloud containers lacked graphics support, Panahi and the Claude Code agent separated simulation from rendering, recording robot poses in the cloud and rendering them locally. They also treated the furniture as static collision objects, which enabled larger runs within the solver’s limits. The robots walked using AI they had already been trained on and followed preset points along a route. Panahi checked how many robots remained upright: In a 256-ward run, 766 of 768 Microducks were still standing after 14 simulated seconds. He said the agent’s work took about two hours. Explore the open source demo for a starter prompt, checks and instructions to begin with one ward on a CPU, then scale to hundreds on an NVIDIA GPU. Create Editable 3D Assets With Houdini and AI Agents 🔗 Creating animated 3D content requires connecting modeling, simulation, materials and rendering. Nick Scarcella, a senior technical artist on NVIDIA’s BondLab team, directed AI agents — primarily using Claude — to work with CUDA libraries and Isaac Sim to create animations. The BondLab team uses SideFX Houdini and the NVIDIA ovrtx library to develop materials, lighting and the final rendered appearance. In one experiment, Scarcella guided Astra to recreate an OP-1 portable synthesizer using product images, manuals and technical direction. He exported the model into the OpenUSD framework, tested it in Houdini and Blender, then used Astra and Opus to refine details before adjusting materials and textures for ovrtx rendering. Scarcella also used a publicly shared robot-hand checkpoint in Isaac Sim, directing the motion and developing materials and lighting in Houdini with Claude’s assistance. Working with team member Steven Dvornik, the team created an “Echos” visualization: translucent versions of the hand overlap and merge into a single hand animation, offering a visual interpretation of robot training. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Robot_Hand_Video_Omniverse.mp4 Figure: An artistic visualization of simulated robot-hand motion, developed with AI assistance and Houdini’s materials and lighting tools. These workflows bring agent-assisted creation into existing artist tools, giving teams editable content they can inspect, refine and render across applications. Explore Scarcella’s Houdini MCP tools and agent skill . Test Robotic Disassembly With Computer-Aided Design and Simulation 🔗 Before a robot can disassemble a product, developers need to know whether its tools can reach and remove the parts. Jens Jebens, a senior product manager for OpenUSD at NVIDIA, directed Astra to model a car suspension in PTC Onshape and configure it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim . Jebens used simulation feedback to revise the tooling, including a wrench designed to reach the suspension’s bolts, and reported successful removal of a suspension component in simulation. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Robotic_Dissasembly_Omniverse.mp4 PTC also connects computer-aided design (CAD) with simulation through Onshape’s SimReady Publisher, built with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Robotics startup Sensori uses it to transfer its Yuri robot into Isaac Sim, carrying geometry, joints and configuration data so the team can evaluate design changes without repeatedly rebuilding the simulation model. Read Sensori’s story . Explore the Onshape importer guide. Create an Editable Building Model From Site Scans 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/relay-video-v14-1080p.mp4 Planning warehouse automation requires a model of the building itself, but shelving and machinery can obscure its structure in site scans. Omniverse brings together real-to-sim tools and agent skills to help developers turn real-world captures into editable starting environments for physical AI simulation. David Wehr, from NVIDIA’s simulation technology team, built on that work using Astra to develop a workflow for digitally reconstructing a building without its contents. The goal is an editable, simulation-ready building model where developers can add or reposition shelving and machinery to evaluate warehouse layouts and automation plans before making physical changes. Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. OpenUSD stores the models, while Omniverse’s ovrtx library renders results for inspection. Explore NVIDIA Omniverse agent skills to help agents build with Omniverse libraries. Test Gas-Turbine Operating Scenarios With a Digital Twin 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Turbine-Lab-RTX-and-What-If-under-10MB-1.mp4 Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator. The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power, efficiency, fuel consumption and equipment response. Six test procedures explore scenarios including load changes, a stuck fuel valve and an exhaust-sensor error. The prototype gives engineers an interactive way to investigate how operating changes and faults could affect equipment behavior, supporting decisions about which scenarios warrant further testing. Astra used tools like Cantera for thermochemistry and SciPy for equipment dynamics. The application maps solver results to rotor animation and color-coded temperature, pressure and flow-velocity indicators in a 3D turbine. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries update the scene ( ovstage ), render it with RTX (ovrtx) and stream the view to the browser (ovstream). Engineers can rotate and zoom the cutaway, switch between indicators, and pause or scrub through a simulated response alongside charts and virtual instruments. Build Simulation Scenes With Open Source SimReady Assets 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/kitchen_final_blog_with_music.mp4 With SimReady Central Library, announced at GTC Berlin , developers can access more than 2,000 simulation-ready USD assets from equipment manufacturers and asset providers for robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins workflows. Paul Kind, a member of NVIDIA’s Omniverse documentation team, pointed an AI agent to the library and guided scene assembly through conversation. His kitchen scene included 180 placements drawn from 63 unique library assets, alongside 18 custom geometry pieces. Kind reviewed renders produced with Isaac Sim and guided further adjustments. For robotics and factory workflows, developers can select SimReady assets with the simulation properties embedded to fit their required task then test in an assembled environment. Find assets in SimReady Central Library , and learn how to contribute . Stress-Test a Warehouse Simulation at Scale 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infra-scale-demo-20260914_144614-Meeting-Recording.mp4 A warehouse simulation needs to keep running smoothly as more robot arms, conveyors and boxes fill the scene. When it slows down, developers need to identify what’s holding it back. Bhavik Sanganee, principal engineer at NVIDIA, used Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build a warehouse simulation, increase its complexity and investigate slowdowns. Performance first fell below the target when the scene doubled in size. Running physics calculations, image rendering and video preparation concurrently restored performance and enabled further scaling. With 80 conveyors, 40 arms and 800 boxes, the simulation sustained 30 frames per second at full HD resolution during a two-minute test. The arms completed 640 successful box placements. Doubling the scene again reduced performance. Testing traced the slowdown to the physics and robot-control pipeline, giving Sanganee a specific area to improve. Start building with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries . Test Robot Control for Flexible Cable Routing 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/scurve_rl_vs_astra_side_by_side.mp4 In electronics assembly, a robot may need to position a flexible cable around components before plugging it into a port. The cable bends as the robot moves it, and the connector must line up precisely to fit. Oyindamola Omotuyi, robotics technical marketing manager at NVIDIA, directed Astra to build a robot simulation using NVIDIA Isaac Lab , Newton physics and Omniverse rendering with a Robotiq gripper handling the cable. Astra also developed a reinforcement learning system that combined learned cable-routing movements with position-and-orientation feedback and corrective adjustments for USB-C insertion. The simulation gave Omotuyi a way to test cable handling and connector alignment before moving to physical-robot experiments. The controller used information supplied directly by the simulation. Next steps include testing a friction-held grasp and using information a physical robot could obtain from cameras and sensors. Get started with robot learning in NVIDIA Isaac Lab . Turn Robot Computer-Aided Design Into a SimReady Asset 🔗 Before testing whether a robot can pick up and move a box, developers need a simulation model with joints that move correctly and with grippers that can hold the object. A computer-aided design (CAD) model provides the robot’s shape, but it still needs physics properties to perform the task. Using an ABB Robotics YuMi robot, developers directed Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse content libraries to convert CAD files into OpenUSD, match the robot’s appearance to reference images, and configure joints and collision geometry. They checked the asset against SimReady Foundation requirements before testing it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Both arms and grippers completed four cube pick-and-place cycles, using simulated finger contact and friction. These tests demonstrated behavior under the simulated conditions — estimated physical properties were not calibrated against the real robot. Follow the five-step SimReady tutorial . Build a Humanoid Simulator for a Warehouse Environment 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Humanoid-Warehouse.mp4 Explore a gamified, physics-based control of a humanoid robot in first- and third-person view. Before automating warehouse tasks, developers need an interactive simulation environment to explore task behavior and evaluate how the work gets done. Frank DeLise, Omniverse product manager at NVIDIA, used Astra to turn a SimReady warehouse and humanoid robot into an interactive simulator with first- and third-person views. DeLise directed Astra to connect NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for physics ( ovphysx ), scene updates ( ovstage ), rendering ( ovrtx ) and the user interface ( ovui ). He also used Astra with SimReady ( simready-foundation ) to create the physical scene in simulation. Astra then generated animation and application code to bring those capabilities together. Learn how to prepare and validate SimReady robot assets with frontier AI models and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Connect an Autonomous-Driving Testing Workflow 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/zero-to-alpamayo-under-10MB.mp4 Changing a scene, sensor or driving model can significantly affect autonomous-vehicle simulations. Doyub Kim, a manager on the simulation technology team at NVIDIA, asked Astra to build Zero to Alpamayo — a reusable simulation environment based on San Francisco’s Market Street. Kim directed Astra to map out the workflow, then connect asset creation, traffic, Omniverse RTX sensor simulation and Alpamayo driving in stages, checking each integration. The resulting prototype was a testing ground for comparing models and tracing how scene or sensor changes affect downstream driving behavior. A separate Cosmos3-Nano experiment varied weather and lighting in recorded simulation videos, allowing Kim to compare the driving model’s responses to the same scenario under different conditions. Use Sensor Differences to Create and Improve Digital Twins 🔗 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/0_00-0_004-hubble_rivermark_Real_Sim_no_loop.mp4 Comparing recorded and simulated camera and lidar outputs gives developers key performance indicator-based feedback for refining a scene. To test robots and autonomous vehicles, developers need to know how closely simulated sensors match real ones. Ashley Reid, who works on RTX sensor validation at NVIDIA, directed Astra and Claude Fable 5 agents to compare ovrtx camera and raw LiDAR outputs with recorded data. The agents created two digital twins from scratch and improved two existing ones. Over about three days, Reid guided an iterative workflow in which agents measured differences, created or modified OpenUSD scenes, and checked the results. Changes addressed missing objects, geometry and materials, with acceptance depending on camera and LiDAR metrics. This gives developers a way to use measured discrepancies to guide scene creation and improvement. Start by rendering an OpenUSD scene with the ovrtx minimal Python example , then define a sensor measure to compare with recorded data. Robo Olympics: Test Robot Skills With Simulation 🔗 Teaching robots new movements means checking whether those actions work under physical constraints. Tae Kim, who leads NVIDIA Omniverse engineering and product, used sports videos and natural-language instructions to guide Astra in building Robo Olympics, an experimental project that tests simulated Unitree G1 humanoids performing sports movements. Under Kim’s direction, Astra built controllers and refined them through physics trials. Newton Physics Engine simulated behavior, the open source NVIDIA Warp framework accelerated calculations and ovrtx rendered scenes and virtual-camera images. In one experiment, the robot cleared a single hurdle in 64 of 100 simulation trials. The trials gave Kim feedback for improving the robot’s timing and control. Watch Kim explore building simulations with Astra and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Bring the International Space Station Into the Browser 🔗 Turning 3D models into an application requires connecting assets, live data and an interface. Nic Johns, an engineering director at NVIDIA, prompted Astra to assemble NASA assets into an OpenUSD International Space Station model with telemetry. Johns built the application with a single prompt, then used a follow-up prompt to shift the scene to Earth’s daytime side so the planet was visible. The workflow used Blender for asset preparation and Omniverse libraries for rendering ( ovrtx ), scene runtime (ovstage) and streaming (ovstream). The application brings 3D models and operational data into the browser, with Johns guiding its development through prompts and corrections. Try the Omniverse Real-Time Viewer skill . Turn Captured Rooms Into Testing Environments 🔗 A digitally reconstructed room needs editable objects and accurate physical behavior before developers can test interactions. Chirag Majithia, from the Isaac engineering applications team at NVIDIA, directed Astra to turn stereo camera captures into an editable OpenUSD studio. The workflow combined PyCuSFM, FoundationStereo and nvblox for reconstruction, with user review guiding object selection and placement. Astra assembled generated and Blender-authored assets and used USD Content Agents to configure how objects move and interact in simulation. Isaac Sim tests guided collision and contact revisions for doors and drawers. The studio connects captured geometry to interaction testing, making gaps and object behavior easier to inspect. Explore USD Content Agents. Have a simulation idea? Explore NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to start building with an AI agent. Build a Voice-Controlled VR Simulation With SimReady Assets Bringing 3D assets into virtual reality (VR) requires more than rendering a scene. Objects need to respond to controllers and behave as expected when grabbed, moved or released. NVIDIA Omniverse community developer Michael Wagner took on this challenge. He directed GPT-6 Astra to use Blender software to model a study environment from two reference images, balancing visual quality with efficient performance in VR. He then used Claude Code to build an application that lets users find SimReady Central assets by voice and interact with them in an immersive VR scene. The Claude Code agent worked for about eight hours, and Wagner built the application over a weekend using an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada workstation and a Meta Quest 3 VR headset. The application ran on NVIDIA Omniverse libraries : ovstage shared the OpenUSD scene, ovrtx rendered it, ovxr enabled VR and ovphysx ran physics. Wagner later built a second version with ovnewton , which integrates with ovstage, to compare the physics libraries. The biggest challenge for Wagner was checking what happened inside the headset. Automated tests missed problems he could feel, including objects shaking when grabbed. Wagner reported the symptoms, guided the agent through changes and verified the interaction himself. Updating the grab control once per frame resolved the shaking. His takeaway: Give agents renders and logs to inspect, then check the experience directly. Explore his open source demo f or build instructions, a starting prompt and reusable agent skills. Send Microducks on Rounds in a Simulated Hospital https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/microducks-icu-16x9-1920x1080-new.mp4 Before adapting a robot to a new environment, developers need to test whether its walking policy — the AI that controls how it moves — can keep it stable in that setting. AI developer Maziyar Panahi directed Claude Code, using Claude Opus 5.5, to assemble an intensive care unit from 13 NVIDIA SimReady hospital assets and test Microduck robots inside it. The assets came with Newton physics settings, so Panahi didn’t have to model the furniture or create collision geometry from scratch. The Newton physics engine also helped replicate the ward so hundreds of copies could run together on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU. When the cloud containers lacked graphics support, Panahi and the Claude Code agent separated simulation from rendering, recording robot poses in the cloud and rendering them locally. They also treated the furniture as static collision objects, which enabled larger runs within the solver’s limits. The robots walked using AI they had already been trained on and followed preset points along a route. Panahi checked how many robots remained upright: In a 256-ward run, 766 of 768 Microducks were still standing after 14 simulated seconds. He said the agent’s work took about two hours. Explore the open source demo for a starter prompt, checks and instructions to begin with one ward on a CPU, then scale to hundreds on an NVIDIA GPU. Create Editable 3D Assets With Houdini and AI Agents Creating animated 3D content requires connecting modeling, simulation, materials and rendering. Nick Scarcella, a senior technical artist on NVIDIA’s BondLab team, directed AI agents — primarily using Claude — to work with CUDA libraries and Isaac Sim to create animations. The BondLab team uses SideFX Houdini and the NVIDIA ovrtx library to develop materials, lighting and the final rendered appearance. In one experiment, Scarcella guided Astra to recreate an OP-1 portable synthesizer using product images, manuals and technical direction. He exported the model into the OpenUSD framework, tested it in Houdini and Blender, then used Astra and Opus to refine details before adjusting materials and textures for ovrtx rendering. Scarcella also used a publicly shared robot-hand checkpoint in Isaac Sim, directing the motion and developing materials and lighting in Houdini with Claude’s assistance. Working with team member Steven Dvornik, the team created an “Echos” visualization: translucent versions of the hand overlap and merge into a single hand animation, offering a visual interpretation of robot training. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Robot_Hand_Video_Omniverse.mp4 Figure: An artistic visualization of simulated robot-hand motion, developed with AI assistance and Houdini’s materials and lighting tools. These workflows bring agent-assisted creation into existing artist tools, giving teams editable content they can inspect, refine and render across applications. Explore Scarcella’s Houdini MCP tools and agent skill . Test Robotic Disassembly With Computer-Aided Design and Simulation Before a robot can disassemble a product, developers need to know whether its tools can reach and remove the parts. Jens Jebens, a senior product manager for OpenUSD at NVIDIA, directed Astra to model a car suspension in PTC Onshape and configure it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim . Jebens used simulation feedback to revise the tooling, including a wrench designed to reach the suspension’s bolts, and reported successful removal of a suspension component in simulation. https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Robotic_Dissasembly_Omniverse.mp4 PTC also connects computer-aided design (CAD) with simulation through Onshape’s SimReady Publisher, built with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Robotics startup Sensori uses it to transfer its Yuri robot into Isaac Sim, carrying geometry, joints and configuration data so the team can evaluate design changes without repeatedly rebuilding the simulation model. Read Sensori’s story . Explore the Onshape importer guide. Create an Editable Building Model From Site Scans https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/relay-video-v14-1080p.mp4 Planning warehouse automation requires a model of the building itself, but shelving and machinery can obscure its structure in site scans. Omniverse brings together real-to-sim tools and agent skills to help developers turn real-world captures into editable starting environments for physical AI simulation. David Wehr, from NVIDIA’s simulation technology team, built on that work using Astra to develop a workflow for digitally reconstructing a building without its contents. The goal is an editable, simulation-ready building model where developers can add or reposition shelving and machinery to evaluate warehouse layouts and automation plans before making physical changes. Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. OpenUSD stores the models, while Omniverse’s ovrtx library renders results for inspection. Explore NVIDIA Omniverse agent skills to help agents build with Omniverse libraries. Test Gas-Turbine Operating Scenarios With a Digital Twin https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Turbine-Lab-RTX-and-What-If-under-10MB-1.mp4 Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator. The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power, efficiency, fuel consumption and equipment response. Six test procedures explore scenarios including load changes, a stuck fuel valve and an exhaust-sensor error. The prototype gives engineers an interactive way to investigate how operating changes and faults could affect equipment behavior, supporting decisions about which scenarios warrant further testing. Astra used tools like Cantera for thermochemistry and SciPy for equipment dynamics. The application maps solver results to rotor animation and color-coded temperature, pressure and flow-velocity indicators in a 3D turbine. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries update the scene ( ovstage ), render it with RTX (ovrtx) and stream the view to the browser (ovstream). Engineers can rotate and zoom the cutaway, switch between indicators, and pause or scrub through a simulated response alongside charts and virtual instruments. Build Simulation Scenes With Open Source SimReady Assets https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/kitchen_final_blog_with_music.mp4 With SimReady Central Library, announced at GTC Berlin , developers can access more than 2,000 simulation-ready USD assets from equipment manufacturers and asset providers for robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins workflows. Paul Kind, a member of NVIDIA’s Omniverse documentation team, pointed an AI agent to the library and guided scene assembly through conversation. His kitchen scene included 180 placements drawn from 63 unique library assets, alongside 18 custom geometry pieces. Kind reviewed renders produced with Isaac Sim and guided further adjustments. For robotics and factory workflows, developers can select SimReady assets with the simulation properties embedded to fit their required task then test in an assembled environment. Find assets in SimReady Central Library , and learn how to contribute . Stress-Test a Warehouse Simulation at Scale https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Infra-scale-demo-20260914_144614-Meeting-Recording.mp4 A warehouse simulation needs to keep running smoothly as more robot arms, conveyors and boxes fill the scene. When it slows down, developers need to identify what’s holding it back. Bhavik Sanganee, principal engineer at NVIDIA, used Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build a warehouse simulation, increase its complexity and investigate slowdowns. Performance first fell below the target when the scene doubled in size. Running physics calculations, image rendering and video preparation concurrently restored performance and enabled further scaling. With 80 conveyors, 40 arms and 800 boxes, the simulation sustained 30 frames per second at full HD resolution during a two-minute test. The arms completed 640 successful box placements. Doubling the scene again reduced performance. Testing traced the slowdown to the physics and robot-control pipeline, giving Sanganee a specific area to improve. Start building with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries . Test Robot Control for Flexible Cable Routing https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/scurve_rl_vs_astra_side_by_side.mp4 In electronics assembly, a robot may need to position a flexible cable around components before plugging it into a port. The cable bends as the robot moves it, and the connector must line up precisely to fit. Oyindamola Omotuyi, robotics technical marketing manager at NVIDIA, directed Astra to build a robot simulation using NVIDIA Isaac Lab , Newton physics and Omniverse rendering with a Robotiq gripper handling the cable. Astra also developed a reinforcement learning system that combined learned cable-routing movements with position-and-orientation feedback and corrective adjustments for USB-C insertion. The simulation gave Omotuyi a way to test cable handling and connector alignment before moving to physical-robot experiments. The controller used information supplied directly by the simulation. Next steps include testing a friction-held grasp and using information a physical robot could obtain from cameras and sensors. Get started with robot learning in NVIDIA Isaac Lab . Turn Robot Computer-Aided Design Into a SimReady Asset Before testing whether a robot can pick up and move a box, developers need a simulation model with joints that move correctly and with grippers that can hold the object. A computer-aided design (CAD) model provides the robot’s shape, but it still needs physics properties to perform the task. Using an ABB Robotics YuMi robot, developers directed Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse content libraries to convert CAD files into OpenUSD, match the robot’s appearance to reference images, and configure joints and collision geometry. They checked the asset against SimReady Foundation requirements before testing it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Both arms and grippers completed four cube pick-and-place cycles, using simulated finger contact and friction. These tests demonstrated behavior under the simulated conditions — estimated physical properties were not calibrated against the real robot. Follow the five-step SimReady tutorial . Build a Humanoid Simulator for a Warehouse Environment https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Humanoid-Warehouse.mp4 Explore a gamified, physics-based control of a humanoid robot in first- and third-person view. Before automating warehouse tasks, developers need an interactive simulation environment to explore task behavior and evaluate how the work gets done. Frank DeLise, Omniverse product manager at NVIDIA, used Astra to turn a SimReady warehouse and humanoid robot into an interactive simulator with first- and third-person views. DeLise directed Astra to connect NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for physics ( ovphysx ), scene updates ( ovstage ), rendering ( ovrtx ) and the user interface ( ovui ). He also used Astra with SimReady ( simready-foundation ) to create the physical scene in simulation. Astra then generated animation and application code to bring those capabilities together. Learn how to prepare and validate SimReady robot assets with frontier AI models and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Connect an Autonomous-Driving Testing Workflow https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/zero-to-alpamayo-under-10MB.mp4 Changing a scene, sensor or driving model can significantly affect autonomous-vehicle simulations. Doyub Kim, a manager on the simulation technology team at NVIDIA, asked Astra to build Zero to Alpamayo — a reusable simulation environment based on San Francisco’s Market Street. Kim directed Astra to map out the workflow, then connect asset creation, traffic, Omniverse RTX sensor simulation and Alpamayo driving in stages, checking each integration. The resulting prototype was a testing ground for comparing models and tracing how scene or sensor changes affect downstream driving behavior. A separate Cosmos3-Nano experiment varied weather and lighting in recorded simulation videos, allowing Kim to compare the driving model’s responses to the same scenario under different conditions. Use Sensor Differences to Create and Improve Digital Twins https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/0_00-0_004-hubble_rivermark_Real_Sim_no_loop.mp4 Comparing recorded and simulated camera and lidar outputs gives developers key performance indicator-based feedback for refining a scene. To test robots and autonomous vehicles, developers need to know how closely simulated sensors match real ones. Ashley Reid, who works on RTX sensor validation at NVIDIA, directed Astra and Claude Fable 5 agents to compare ovrtx camera and raw LiDAR outputs with recorded data. The agents created two digital twins from scratch and improved two existing ones. Over about three days, Reid guided an iterative workflow in which agents measured differences, created or modified OpenUSD scenes, and checked the results. Changes addressed missing objects, geometry and materials, with acceptance depending on camera and LiDAR metrics. This gives developers a way to use measured discrepancies to guide scene creation and improvement. Start by rendering an OpenUSD scene with the ovrtx minimal Python example , then define a sensor measure to compare with recorded data. Robo Olympics: Test Robot Skills With Simulation Teaching robots new movements means checking whether those actions work under physical constraints. Tae Kim, who leads NVIDIA Omniverse engineering and product, used sports videos and natural-language instructions to guide Astra in building Robo Olympics, an experimental project that tests simulated Unitree G1 humanoids performing sports movements. Under Kim’s direction, Astra built controllers and refined them through physics trials. Newton Physics Engine simulated behavior, the open source NVIDIA Warp framework accelerated calculations and ovrtx rendered scenes and virtual-camera images. In one experiment, the robot cleared a single hurdle in 64 of 100 simulation trials. The trials gave Kim feedback for improving the robot’s timing and control. Watch Kim explore building simulations with Astra and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Bring the International Space Station Into the Browser Turning 3D models into an application requires connecting assets, live data and an interface. Nic Johns, an engineering director at NVIDIA, prompted Astra to assemble NASA assets into an OpenUSD International Space Station model with telemetry. Johns built the application with a single prompt, then used a follow-up prompt to shift the scene to Earth’s daytime side so the planet was visible. The workflow used Blender for asset preparation and Omniverse libraries for rendering ( ovrtx ), scene runtime (ovstage) and streaming (ovstream). The application brings 3D models and operational data into the browser, with Johns guiding its development through prompts and corrections. Try the Omniverse Real-Time Viewer skill . Turn Captured Rooms Into Testing Environments A digitally reconstructed room needs editable objects and accurate physical behavior before developers can test interactions. Chirag Majithia, from the Isaac engineering applications team at NVIDIA, directed Astra to turn stereo camera captures into an editable OpenUSD studio. The workflow combined PyCuSFM, FoundationStereo and nvblox for reconstruction, with user review guiding object selection and placement. Astra assembled generated and Blender-authored assets and used USD Content Agents to configure how objects move and interact in simulation. Isaac Sim tests guided collision and contact revisions for doors and drawers. The studio connects captured geometry to interaction testing, making gaps and object behavior easier to inspect. Explore USD Content Agents. Have a simulation idea? Explore NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to start building with an AI agent.

title: 15 Members And Associates Of Gorilla Stone Bloods Gang Charged With Narcotics And Firearms Offenses In Sara D. Roosevelt Park
body: Press Release 15 Members And Associates Of Gorilla Stone Bloods Gang Charged With Narcotics And Firearms Offenses In Sara D. Roosevelt Park Thursday, November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Southern District of New York United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Jamie McDonald, Acting Special Agent in Charge of the New York Field Office of Homeland Security Investigations (“HSI”), Pete Gizas, Special Agent in Charge of the New York Task Force Division of the Drug Enforcement Administration (“DEA”), Christopher Roberts, and Commissioner of the New York City Police Department (“NYPD”), Jessica S. Tisch, announced today the unsealing of an Indictment charging 15 members and associates of the Untouchable Gorilla Stone Nation (“Gorilla Stone”), a set of the nationwide Bloods street gang, with conspiring to distribute crack cocaine, heroin, fentanyl, and synthetic cannabinoids in and around Sara D. Roosevelt Park (“SDR Park”) in the Lower East Side of Manhattan.  Some defendants were additionally charged with possessing firearms, some of which were brandished and discharged, in furtherance of their narcotics trafficking.  Six of the defendants were in New York City or New York State custody and brought into federal custody, with eight of the remaining nine defendants arrested and presented in federal court.  The case is assigned to U.S. District Judge Lewis J. Liman. “Our Office will stop at nothing to keep New Yorkers and our community safe,” said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald.  “This is particularly true for public spaces in New York, like our parks. As alleged, for years a violent gang network operated an open-air drug market that poisoned the Lower East Side of Manhattan with fentanyl, heroin, crack cocaine, and K2.  The defendants allegedly trafficked deadly drugs while arming themselves with illegal firearms and engaging in brutal violence to protect their turf.  Gang-driven narcotics trafficking inflicts enormous harm on neighborhoods and families. New Yorkers should know that they can count on our Office and our law enforcement partners to protect them from these harms.” “Today’s arrests strike a major blow against this gang who is accused of using fear, violence, narcotics sales, and illegal guns to control the streets and parks of a New York City community,” said HSI Acting Special Agent in Charge Pete Gizas.  “New Yorkers deserve safe neighborhoods, not ones ruled by violent criminal organizations.  We will combat these violent gangs with decisive law enforcement might.  HSI New York, alongside the U.S. Attorney’s Office, NYPD, DEA, and all our law enforcement partners, will relentlessly pursue those responsible and hold them accountable.” “All New Yorkers deserve the right to live, work, and enjoy public spaces and parks free from drugs, gangs, and violence,” said DEA New York Task Force Division Special Agent in Charge Christopher Roberts.  “These defendants allegedly turned the Sara D. Roosevelt Park into an open-air drug market, using fear, intimidation, and brutal violence to control areas of the park and terrorize this community.  From vicious slashings and stabbings to shootings and armed assaults, these violent acts demonstrated the dangerous lengths these individuals used to protect their criminal enterprise and exert control over our neighborhoods.  Today, those days are over!  The DEA and our law enforcement partners will not stand idle while violent gangs attempt to take over our parks and neighborhoods.  Our public spaces belong to the people, not drug traffickers and criminals.” “As alleged, these defendants, part of the Untouchable Gorilla Stone Nation gang, turned a Lower East Side park into their own open-air drug market and violent playground,” said NYPD Commissioner Jessica S. Tisch.  “This takedown is yet another example of the diligent work our investigators do to dismantle dangerous gangs and stop the illegal drug businesses that threaten our communities.  I thank our dedicated NYPD detectives, law enforcement partners, and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York for their shared commitment to making New York City safer.” According to the Indictment and public court filings:(1) Between approximately 2023 and 2026, the defendants were members or associates of the Gorilla Stone gang and took over SDR Park, in the heart of the Lower East Side, with violence and fear through the trafficking of crack cocaine, heroin, fentanyl, and synthetic cannabinoids or K2.  The defendants had established agreements, understandings, and practices that governed how they operated and how their different members coexisted within the same drug-dealing territory.  For example, the defendants divided SDR Park, with certain dealers controlling different parts of the Park.  While these dealers permitted one another to sell in close physical proximity, they did not allow outsiders or newcomers to sell in their territory and worked together, often using violence to keep out rival or unfamiliar drug dealers.  The defendants also exercised control over the Park by working in shifts.  By agreement and with proactive coordination, certain dealers, along with their workers, sold in the morning, while others sold in the evening or overnight.  In addition, the defendants warned each other about law enforcement’s presence in the area, shared suppliers (and several defendants and other members of the conspiracy themselves supplied narcotics to other defendants), steered customers to each other, provided each other with narcotics when someone ran out, and jointly responded to threats that might impact any dealer in SDR Park. To protect and further its drug business, certain of the defendants engaged in frequent acts of violence, including committing slashings, stabbings, robberies, and gun violence against rival drug dealers in the area and their own narcotics customers, typically drug-addicted individuals.  For instance: In December 2024, in the vicinity of SDR Park, Ibrahim Toure, a/k/a “Fah,” sold K2 to a customer who paid Toure with counterfeit cash.  Toure slashed the victim twice, once to the top of his head and once to his face, as depicted below. In February 2026, in the vicinity of SDR Park, Matthew Newman, a/k/a “Money,” participated in the stabbing of a victim whose close friend had a narcotics-related debt to Newman.  Specifically, Newman gave a blade to an uncharged coconspirator, who stabbed the victim seven times in the back, resulting in a collapsed lung and bleeding from a kidney. In April 2026, in the vicinity of SDR Park, Newman, Basil Simms, a/k/a “Sheff,” Sean Sims, a/k/a “Vito,” and one unidentified perpetrator assaulted and stabbed another drug dealer who was selling K2 at under-market prices.  A photo of the victim’s leg is depicted below. In July 2026, CAMERON BARNHILL, a/k/a “Baby Ape,” and ASHANTE INNISS, a/k/a “Fire,” with other perpetrators, assaulted and robbed a competitor drug dealer near SDR Park, including by stomping on his face and neck and by beating him with a traffic cone.  A screenshot of the assault is depicted below: In May 2024, NEWMAN, with two other perpetrators, committed a gang-related assault, including a pistol-whipping, of another Gorilla Stone member who was perceived to be a disfavored member of the gang.  Screenshots of NEWMAN committing the gang assault, which took place near SDR Park, are depicted below: Several members of Gorilla Stone, including some of the defendants, also possessed and carried firearms in and around SDR Park, including to have firearms available in the event of a dispute.  For example, from approximately 2024 to 2025, Sims, then a member of another Bloods set, engaged in a series of back-and-forth acts of violence with Newman regarding, among other things, their respective drug-dealing territory and influence in SDR Park.  Following a March 2025 incident in which Newman and Sims slashed each other, Sims determined that he wanted to join Gorilla Stone to avoid continued fighting with Newman.  Newman provided Sims with a gun and told him to shoot an enemy of Gorilla Stone.  On or about April 19, 2026, Sims and an uncharged coconspirator shot a 16-year-old victim in the upper thigh, as depicted below.  The victim was hospitalized. *                *                * A chart containing the defendants’ names, charges, and maximum penalties is set forth below. The maximum potential sentences in this case are prescribed by Congress and provided here for informational purposes only, as any sentencing of the defendants will be determined by the judge. Mr. McDonald thanked HSI, DEA, and the NYPD for their exceptional investigative work, as well as the Digital Forensics Unit, and the Complex Analytics and Social Media Enhancement Team at the New York/New Jersey High Intensity Drug Trafficking Area of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York.  Mr. McDonald further thanked the United States Marshals Service for their assistance and partnership. This case is being handled by the Office’s Narcotics Unit.  Assistant U.S. Attorneys Remy Grosbard, Kevin Grossinger, Mostafa Khairy, and Lauren E. Phillips are in charge of the prosecution. The charges contained in the Indictment are merely accusations, and the defendants are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty. title: Former Hacienda Employee Sentenced to 50 Months in Prison for His Participation in a Bribery Conspiracy Involving Loss of $5 Million
body: Press Release Former Hacienda Employee Sentenced to 50 Months in Prison for His Participation in a Bribery Conspiracy Involving Loss of $5 Million Thursday, November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Puerto Rico SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico – On November 18, 2026, United States District Court Judge Silvia Carreño Coll sentenced former Hacienda employee Luis A. Jiménez-Guzmán to 50 months in prison, two years of supervised release, and restitution of 5 million dollars for his role in a bribery conspiracy to defraud the Puerto Rico Department of Treasury (PRDT or Hacienda), announced Héctor Ramírez Carbó, Acting United States Attorney for the District of Puerto Rico.  On July 2, 2026, Jiménez-Guzmán was charged and pleaded guilty to a bribery conspiracy involving the loss of approximately $5,000,000 in Puerto Rico tax revenue, in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 371. According to the plea agreement in the case, Luis A. Jiménez-Guzmán, knowingly and willfully conspired to commit federal program bribery and wire fraud, as well as accepted bribe payments in exchange for his corrupt acts. From February 2019 through March 2023, Jiménez-Guzmán was an employee and agent of the PRDT with duties that included physically and electronically accessing and reviewing tax returns and documents related to invoicing and collection of owed taxes. The defendant had privileged access to the PRDT’s online platforms, the Puerto Rico Integrated Tax Administration System (PRITAS) and the Internal Revenue Unified System (GenTax/SURI) and was able to access, monitor, and modify taxpayer information, including creating taxpayer credits, modifying income tax, employee retention tax and sales tax information. As part of the bribery conspiracy, Jiménez-Guzmán corruptly accepted cash payments and other benefits, in exchange for submitting false information to the PRDT. The false information was submitted to the PRDT for the elimination of taxes owed, evasion of taxes, and theft of funds. For example, on August 16, 2021, Jiménez-Guzmán received a $10,000 bribe payment from Person H to erase and reduce a tax debt of one of Person H’s customers. The illicit payments were solicited and accepted by Jiménez-Guzmán, who illegally eliminated the PRDT tax liabilities and obtained illegal tax refunds for several individual and business taxpayers, with a total approximate loss to the PRDT of $5,000,000. Acting U.S. Attorney Héctor Ramírez-Carbó of the District of Puerto Rico; and Carlos R. Goris, Special Agent in Charge of FBI San Juan Field Office made the announcement. The Federal Bureau of Investigation investigated these matters. Assistant U.S. Attorney Marie Christine Amy from the District of Puerto Rico’s Financial Fraud & Public Corruption Section prosecuted this case. This is part of an ongoing effort to combat public corruption and fraud committed by Puerto Rico Department of Treasury employees. The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Puerto Rico previously announced the indictment of twenty-six individuals and corporations in October 2025 and the guilty pleas of three Hacienda employees, Luis A. Jiménez-Guzmán , Harry E. Mueriel-Falero , and Alexander Ortiz-Robles . # # # Updated November 19, 2026 Topics Fraud Financial Fraud Public Corruption Components Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) USAO - Puerto Rico Press Release Number: 2026-126

title: New York City Man Pleads Guilty to Sending a White Powder Letter to the Superintendent of the Coxsackie Correctional Facility
body: Press Release New York City Man Pleads Guilty to Sending a White Powder Letter to the Superintendent of the Coxsackie Correctional Facility Thursday, November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of New York USANYN-MediaInquiry@usa.doj.gov On November 12, 2026, James McDonaugh, age 49, of Manhattan, New York, pled guilty to conveying a hoax involving a white powder letter.  First Assistant United States Attorney John A. Sarcone III and Craig L. Tremaroli, Special Agent in Charge of the Albany Field Office for the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), made the announcement. As part of his guilty plea, McDonaugh admitted that on December 17, 2024, while serving as an inmate at the Coxsackie Correctional Facility, he used the prison’s internal mail system to send an envelope to the prison’s Superintendent.  The envelope contained a letter and some white powder.  The letter said “ANtrax DIE BITCH”. McDonaugh further admitted that he intended to scare members of the Superintendent’s staff into believing that anthrax, a dangerous biological agent, was in the envelope. McDonaugh faces up to five years of imprisonment, a $250,000 fine, and up to three years of supervised release. A defendant’s sentence is imposed by a judge based on the particular statute(s) the defendant is convicted of violating, the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other factors. Sentencing is currently scheduled for March 15, 2027, at 12:30 pm in Albany, New York, before U.S. District Judge, Elizabeth C. Coombe. First Assistant United States Attorney John A. Sarcone III said: “Using white powder letter hoaxes to scare members of law enforcement who are simply doing their job will not be tolerated by my office. Mr. McDonaugh’s actions have earned him some additional time behind bars.” “Mr. McDonaugh’s reckless decision to send a hoax white powder letter through the prison’s mail system just extended his stay behind bars,” said Craig Tremaroli, Special Agent in Charge of the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Albany Field Office. “The FBI takes hoax threats very seriously and will continue to work with our law enforcement partners to ensure anyone who tries to cause fear and chaos through these calculated actions is brought to justice. The FBI investigated the case with assistance from the New York State Department of Corrections and Community Supervision.  Assistant U.S. Attorney Rick Belliss is prosecuting the case. title: 13 Defendants Arrested on Federal Indictment Charging Them With Stealing More Than $22.5 Million in Consumer Goods from Trains
body: Press Release 13 Defendants Arrested on Federal Indictment Charging Them With Stealing More Than $22.5 Million in Consumer Goods from Trains Thursday, November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Central District of California LOS ANGELES – 13 defendants were arrested today on a 17-count federal indictment charging them with burglarizing at least three dozen trains and stealing more than $22 million worth of Nike sneakers, Milwaukee tools, and other products, then selling them on the black market, coordinating their thefts via Instagram. “The scale of the theft is staggering. We have charged a crew of 14 in a scheme to steal more than $22.5 million in cargo from at least three dozen freight trains in Southern California,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli. “We will prosecute the people who raid these trains and those who knowingly turn stolen cargo into cash.” “This historic indictment, following a 14-month investigation assisted by our Bureau of Investigation, demonstrates the importance of dismantling entire criminal enterprises — from those stealing the cargo to those profiting from its resale,” Los Angeles County Nathan J. Hochman said. “We are determined to protect this vital supply chain and ensure that goods reach their intended destinations, not the black market.” The following defendants charged today are expected to make their initial appearances and be arraigned on the indictment this afternoon in United States District Court in downtown Los Angeles: Nathan Daniel Angel, 21, of East Los Angeles, the crew’s leader; Daniel Angel, 38, a.k.a. “Rayo,” of East Los Angeles, Nathan Angel’s father; Rodolfo Angel, 23, a.k.a. “Rudy” and “Flaco,” of East Los Angeles, Nathan Angel’s uncle; Jose Luis Angel, 23, a.k.a. “Joe,” of East Los Angeles, Nathan Angel’s uncle; Donta Hedgeman, 27, a.k.a. “Dret,” of East Los Angeles; Fernando Alexis Alvarado Villegas, 27, of the Historic South-Central neighborhood of Los Angeles; Daniel Garcia, 36, of East Los Angeles; Carlos Robert Estrada, 28, a.k.a. “JD,” of Whittier; Angel Sanchez, 24, a.k.a. “Fluffy,” of Commerce; Ruben Mario Banuelos, 26, a.k.a. “Bubu,” of East Los Angeles; Fredy Marquina, 25, of the Westlake neighborhood of Los Angeles; Carlos Luis Fernando Martinez, 23, of the Vermont Square area of South Los Angeles; Jorge Angel Aguilar Espinoza, 36, of East Los Angeles; Ricardo Mares, 32, of the Florence-Firestone area of Los Angeles. The federal grand jury charged all 14 defendants with one count of conspiracy. The indictment further charges 14 counts of theft of interstate railroad cargo and possession or receipt of stolen interstate railroad cargo, and two counts of violence against railroad carriers. According to the indictment, shipping containers with Nike sneakers and other freight routinely enter the United States from international destinations via the Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach then are transported by trains operated by carrier companies for further distribution throughout the U.S. From February 2024 to August 2026, Nathan Angel targeted high-value trains traveling through Southern California carrying Nike sneakers and other products, intending to steal them and resell them on the black market. At his direction, Daniel Angel, Rodolfo Angel, Jose Angel, Villegas, Estrada, and Sanchez rented or used trucks and vans to drive burglars to the railroad tracks, where the burglars boarded the trains. These co-defendants also acted as lookouts. Nathan Angel and other co-conspirators pre-determined locations along the tracks to disable the trains. Hedgeman and other co-conspirators then cut the air hoses of the trains, forcing the trains to come to an emergency stop. Daniel Angel, Rodolfo Angel, Jose Angel, Villegas, Estrada, and Sanchez met the train burglars where they had disabled the trains and helped load stolen train cargo into trucks and vans, which they then transported to stash houses, including the residences of Villegas, Garcia, and Daniel Angel. The burglaries occurred on railroad tracks in Pico Rivera, Fullerton, and other locations in Southern California. Nathan Angel alerted Garcia about the type of products that had been stolen from the trains. They would then discuss resale prices for the stolen products. Nathan Angel sent to Marquina, Martinez, and Espinoza photographs of the stolen Nike sneakers and other products, often while the trains were being burglarized. These co-defendants knowingly took the stolen products into their possession. Marquina then contacted potential buyers, including representatives of a business identified in the indictment as  “Company 1,” a sneaker and streetwear resale brand with headquarters in Los Angeles that was not an authorized Nike reseller. Marquina and Martinez sold the stolen Nike sneakers and other products to Company 1, which then sold the stolen products for a profit. From May 2025 to October 2025, Marquina and Martinez sold thousands of pairs of stolen Nike sneakers, many in their original Nike factory cartons, to Company 1 and received from Company 1 a total of approximately $1,081,493 for the stolen Nike products and other stolen items. Espinoza also obtained stolen Nike sneakers and other stolen goods from suppliers, including Nathan Angel. Garcia helped deliver the stolen goods to Espinoza’s residence, where Espinoza stored them. Espinoza advertised the stolen goods to potential buyers, including on social media accounts. He then sold the stolen goods to buyers for a profit. An indictment contains allegations that a defendant has committed a crime. Every defendant is presumed to be innocent until and unless proven guilty in court. If convicted, the defendants would face a statutory maximum sentence of five years in federal prison for the conspiracy count, up to 10 years in federal prison for each theft count, and a statutory maximum sentence of life in federal prison for each violence against railroad cars count. Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the Los Angeles Police Department Commercial Crimes Bureau, the Union Pacific Railroad Police Department, and the California Highway Patrol Cargo Theft Interdiction Program, with assistance from IRS Criminal Investigation, are investigating this matter. Assistant United States Attorney Diane Roldán and Eric Mackie of the Major Crimes Section is prosecuting this case, with assistance from the Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office. title: Norway Man Pleads Guilty to Burglarizing a Gun Store and Illegally Possessing Firearms
body: Press Release Norway Man Pleads Guilty to Burglarizing a Gun Store and Illegally Possessing Firearms Thursday, November 19, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               District of Maine Grover Lee Harmon stole 12 firearms PORTLAND, Maine: A Norway man pleaded guilty today in U.S. District Court in Portland to stealing firearms from a federally licensed firearms dealer and being a felon in possession of a firearm. According to court records, in March 2026, 12 handguns were stolen from J&K Sporting Goods in West Paris, a federally licensed firearms dealer. In April 2026, Grover Lee Harmon , 41, was arrested on unrelated warrants during a traffic stop. A search of Harmon’s vehicle revealed three pistol magazines. Investigators subsequently executed a search warrant at a residence used by Harmon and his girlfriend and located two of the firearms stolen in the March burglary. During an interview with investigators, Harmon admitted to being part of the gun store burglary, and acknowledged he handled the firearms after they were taken from the store. Harmon is prohibited from possessing firearms as a result of a prior felony conviction. For the theft charge, Harmon faces up to five years in prison, up to a $250,000 fine, and a maximum supervised release term of three years. For the illegal possession of a firearm charge, Harmon faces up to 15 years in prison, up to a $250,000 fine, and a maximum supervised release term of three years. title: Outdoor Recreation Economic Statistics, U.S. and States, 2025
body: News Release Explore Product View News Release Related Materials Contacts EMBARGOED UNTIL RELEASE AT 10:00 a.m. EST, Wednesday, November 18, 2026 BEA 26–48 Outdoor Recreation Economic Statistics, U.S. and States, 2025 New Statistics for 2025; Updates for 2021–2024 Today, the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis released new statistics measuring the outdoor recreation economy for the nation, all 50 states, and the District of Columbia. The new data show that the value added of the outdoor recreation economy accounted for 2.3 percent ($704.2 billion) of current-dollar gross domestic product (GDP) for the nation in 2025 (national table 2). Across states and the District of Columbia, value added for outdoor recreation as a share of state GDP ranged from 6.1 percent in Hawaii to 1.0 percent in the District of Columbia (state table 1). Inflation-adjusted (“real”) GDP for the outdoor recreation economy increased 1.9 percent in 2025, compared with an increase of 2.3 percent for the overall U.S. economy, reflecting a deceleration from the 2.5 percent increase in 2024 (national table 1). In 2025, real gross output for the outdoor recreation economy increased 2.1 percent, compensation increased 4.6 percent, and employment increased 1.7 percent (national table 9). Outdoor recreation employment increased in 43 states and the District of Columbia in 2025. The change in outdoor recreation employment ranged from 5.0 percent in Rhode Island, Kansas, and the District of Columbia to −1.1 percent in New Jersey and Alabama ( BEA interactive tables ). Outdoor recreation by activity Outdoor recreation activities fall into three general categories: (1) conventional activities such as bicycling, boating, hiking, and hunting; (2) other activities such as gardening and outdoor concerts; and (3) supporting activities such as construction, travel and tourism, local trips, and government expenditures. In 2025, conventional outdoor recreation accounted for 29.2 percent of U.S. outdoor recreation value added, compared with 29.1 percent in 2024. “Other outdoor recreation” accounted for 19.3 percent of value added in 2025, compared with 19.1 percent in 2024. Supporting outdoor recreation accounted for 51.5 percent of value added in 2025, compared with 51.7 percent in 2024. Additional highlights for value added by activity for 2025 include (state table 2): Boating/fishing was the largest conventional activity for the nation at $39.1 billion in current-dollar value added and was the largest conventional activity in 35 states and the District of Columbia. The states with the largest contributions were Florida ($4.5 billion), California ($3.3 billion), and Texas ($3.0 billion). RVing was the second-largest conventional activity for the nation at $26.8 billion in current-dollar value added and was the largest conventional activity in 10 states. The states with the largest contributions were Indiana ($4.7 billion), Texas ($2.6 billion), and California ($2.1 billion). Hunting/shooting/trapping was the third-largest conventional activity for the nation at $15.1 billion in current-dollar value added and was the largest conventional activity in Arizona and Wyoming. The states with the largest contributions were Texas ($1.8 billion), California ($849.8 million), and Florida ($831.3 million). Snow activities for the nation totaled $7.8 billion in current-dollar value added and was the largest conventional activity in Colorado, Utah, and Vermont. The states with the largest contributions were Colorado ($1.8 billion), California ($735.7 million), and Utah ($640.1 million). Outdoor recreation by industry The outdoor recreation by industry data show the contributions of industries to the outdoor recreation economy, including their impact on value added, gross output, employment, and compensation. For the nation, the arts, entertainment, recreation, accommodation, and food services industry group was the largest contributor to U.S. outdoor recreation in 2025, accounting for $179.5 billion, or 25.5 percent of current-dollar value added. At the state level, arts, entertainment, recreation, accommodation, and food services was the largest contributor to outdoor recreation value added in 25 states and the District of Columbia. The states with the largest contributions were California ($23.5 billion), Florida ($23.4 billion), and New York ($11.6 billion) (state table 3). Retail trade was the second-largest industry group for the nation, at $166.5 billion, or 23.6 percent of value added, and was the largest industry group in 22 states. The states with the largest contributions were California ($19.5 billion), Texas ($14.6 billion), and Florida ($13.3 billion). Transportation and warehousing was the third-largest industry group for the nation, at $86.4 billion, or 12.3 percent of value added, and was the largest industry group in Alaska. The states with the largest contributions were Florida ($12.8 billion), California ($10.8 billion), and Texas ($7.1 billion). Annual update of outdoor recreation economic statistics Estimates for 2021 to 2024 were updated to incorporate newly available and revised source data. At the national level, gross output, value added, employment, and compensation reflect the results of the 2026 annual update of the National Economic Accounts, which include the National Income and Product Accounts and the Industry Economic Accounts. The state statistics now reflect these updated national data as well as the 2026 annual update of the Regional Economic Accounts and newly available and revised regional source data. Previously published estimates are available in BEA’s Data Archive . title: NVIDIA RTX Spark Compact Desktops Out Now
body: NVIDIA RTX Spark Compact Desktops Out Now Systems from ASUS, Dell and MSI are now available — with more from Acer, GIGABYTE, HP and Microsoft on the way — bringing RTX acceleration and up to 128GB of unified memory to local AI, development and creative workflows. November 18, 2026 by Justin Walker 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! New NVIDIA RTX Spark compact desktops from ASUS, Dell and MSI are available today, bringing local AI agents, image and video generation, and model fine-tuning to a dedicated Windows PC. With up to 128GB of unified memory and NVIDIA’s AI software stack, these systems provide room for larger local models alongside RTX-accelerated creative and development tools. A dedicated desktop can keep agents and scheduled tasks running while a laptop travels or handles other work. Alongside the new desktops, an expanding software ecosystem brings more creative and development workflows to RTX Spark laptops and compact desktops. Native Windows on Arm applications from Adobe, the NVIDIA DLSS Ray Reconstruction feature in Blender and local generation workflows in ComfyUI expand what creators and developers can do on RTX Spark — all on one Windows PC. A Windows PC Built for Local AI As workflows expand to include local AI models and agents, more work can continue beyond an active editing session — from generating assets to processing long renders or scheduled tasks. RTX Spark compact desktops give developers, creators and AI enthusiasts a dedicated Windows PC for local models and always-on agents. They bring together image and video generation, model fine-tuning, creative applications and development tools in one compact system. Running supported models locally keeps locally processed code and files on the PC and avoids per-token cloud application programming interface (API) charges for those tasks. RTX Spark compact desktops like the ASUS ProArt GR1X mini PC are built to run personal AI agents 24/7. RTX Spark desktops are equipped with a 20-core NVIDIA Grace CPU, an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU with 6,144 CUDA cores and up to 128GB of unified memory, delivering up to 1 petaflop of AI performance. Ten-gigabit Ethernet connectivity enables fast transfers of large datasets, model files and creative assets between RTX Spark compact desktops and networked storage. This advanced hardware unlocks incredible capabilities for creators, developers and AI enthusiasts, including: Running massive 120-billion-parameter large language models locally Rendering 90GB+ 3D scenes in real time Smoothly editing 4:2:2 video in real time The MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ Series RTX Spark compact desktop. New compact desktops are available for purchase from ASUS, Dell and MSI, joining the RTX Spark family of laptops available today. Mini PCs from Acer, GIGABYTE and HP are coming soon, along with the Microsoft Surface RTX Spark Dev Box . From Local Agents to AI Creation Native CUDA support and Linux development tools through Windows Subsystem for Linux give developers a foundation for building and running local AI workflows. Developers can set up agents with Hermes Agent or NVIDIA NemoClaw blueprints and fine-tune supported models using Unsloth. RTX Spark can run creative agents that connect familiar applications and local AI tools, helping creators move from an idea to finished work with natural-language instructions. NVIDIA Switchyard, now available in Hermes, automatically routes agent tasks between local and cloud models. Everyday tasks can run on device, while advanced reasoning draws on cloud models, helping manage cloud costs across creative workflows. These capabilities come together in creative workflows that connect Photoshop and ComfyUI through Hermes Agent. Using natural-language instructions, creators can turn sketches into rendered images and animations, or animate an image entirely on device — from isolating a subject and defining its motion to generating the finished video. NVIDIA brought these workflows to life at Adobe MAX, where attendees used natural-language instructions to turn sketches into rendered images and animations for a shared digital Miami landscape. The RTX Video Frame Generation and RTX Video HDR features, already available in ComfyUI, extend the pipeline: a generated clip can be expanded to 60 frames per second and converted to high dynamic range for color grading, all within a single ComfyUI workflow on RTX Spark. Adobe Accelerates the Full Creative Stack for RTX Spark NVIDIA and Adobe are expanding native Windows on Arm support and RTX acceleration across Adobe’s creative applications, helping video editors, photographers, designers and 3D artists work more efficiently on RTX Spark. Adobe Premiere accelerates a range of AI-powered editing features through NVIDIA TensorRT-RTX , including Enhance Speech, Object Mask, Scene Edit Detection and Auto Reframe — so editors spend less time waiting and more time cutting. GPU acceleration also extends to Film Impact transition and effects plug-ins. The update improves support for professional video formats, including Canon RAW, Red RAW, ARRI RAW, ARRICORE, ARRI HDE, H.264 and HEVC in MXF, ProRes RAW and long-GOP video. This lets editors realize more than 50% quicker turnaround on everyday H.264 video deliverables. Adobe Photoshop adds TensorRT-RTX acceleration for the Remove Tool and ArmRTX Spark-native Camera Raw support, helping photographers remove unwanted objects faster and work with RAW images without relying on emulation. At Adobe MAX, Adobe previewed a next-generation image processing engine with extensive GPU acceleration, including interactive Gaussian blur and Light Leaks filters. Adobe Substance 3D Painter 12.2 is now optimized for RTX Spark with native support on Arm for the first time in public beta. Artists in games, visual effects and visualization can run Substance Painter natively on RTX Spark laptops and compact desktops, with no compatibility layer required. Adobe Illustrator and InDesign now offer native Windows on Arm versions optimized for RTX Spark. Adobe Illustrator delivers up to 30% higher performance than its emulated version, helping accelerate illustration, graphic design and page-layout workflows on RTX Spark. Blender 5.3 Adds DLSS Ray Reconstruction to the Viewport Blender 5.3 integrates DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction into the Cycles viewport, helping artists evaluate lighting and materials with near-final-quality ray-traced previews as they work. The practical difference is immediate: instead of navigating a noisy, resolving preview, Ray Reconstruction delivers near-final-quality lighting, reflections and materials in the interactive viewport in real time. DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction support requires Blender 5.3 and the latest NVIDIA Game Ready Driver or NVIDIA Studio Driver. Download the NVIDIA App to get automatic notifications when the latest drivers are available, optimize games and applications from a unified GPU control center, and discover the latest NVIDIA tools and software. Windows Server 2028 Coming to DGX Station for Windows Announced at Microsoft Ignite, Windows Server is evolving for organizations that need to run AI closer to their enterprise applications and data. Microsoft is expanding hardware choice through support for the latest AI silicon, helping customers take advantage of accelerated inference and increasingly capable models in their own environments. NVIDIA DGX Station for Windows platform powered by the GB300 Grace Blackwell Ultra Desktop Superchip is expanding to include support for Windows Server 2028. New accelerator platforms and the breadth of the Windows silicon ecosystem provide customers options at different capability levels and price points for advanced AI development, local inference, and agent workloads at scale. Windows ML Updates Give Developers More Options Also announced at Microsoft Ignite, developers can now bring any GGUF model from Hugging Face and run it within Windows ML using the llama.cpp backend. The DxCGC backend, now available as an experimental release, is an integration for game developers that compiles and runs machine learning models through DirectX 12, allowing them to execute AI workloads alongside graphics. Windows APIs let applications integrate platform-provided AI capabilities adding GPU support for AION Instruct and VSR. Developers can also build high-performance AI models for Windows ML using the command line interface. #ICYMI: The Latest NVIDIA Local AI Updates 🦙 llama.cpp v1.0.0 marks a major milestone for building local AI apps. The open source inference engine introduces API versioning updates, alongside expanded model support and CUDA optimizations for NVFP4 inference. Learn more . 🎉 Ricursive Intelligence introduced its first open model: Ripple-65B Preview. The full-stack AI lab builds self-improving systems by co-optimizing hardware, software and models. Ripple-65B Preview was trained on NVIDIA B300 GPUs, refined using NVIDIA Nemotron post-training datasets and runs locally on DGX Spark. Download the NVFP4 checkpoint from Hugging Face . 🤖 Runway’s Praxis-1 is a newly released 27-billion-parameter world action model that predicts video and actions together. Developers can run it locally on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090, NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, DGX Spark and DGX Station, and adapt it to their own robots, cameras and tasks with LoRA fine-tuning. Download the NVFP4 checkpoint from Hugging Face . 🛠️ NVIDIA TensorRT Edge-LLM helps run AI models locally on DGX Spark with just a few commands. Read the technical blog , which walks through downloading Nemotron-3.5 Lightning, setting up optimized inference, testing prompts and serving the model through a local OpenAI-compatible API.
